2.overview:
Four words open the chapter and they are the difference between this king and the last one: David inquired of the LORD. He is holding the dead king's crown, he has Samuel's anointing behind him, Saul and his heir are dead and the northern army is destroyed — and there is no living person whose permission he needs. He asks anyway. Then, given a yes, he asks a second question rather than let the first answer cover it. Set that against David said in his heart at 1 Sam. 27:1, which cost him sixteen months in enemy country.

His first act as king is a thank-you letter to Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul — the town that walked all night through occupied territory to take four bodies off a Philistine wall, because of one night forty years earlier when the Spirit came on a young man behind a plough. David names what they did with the covenant word and asks God to do the same for them. It is entirely genuine, and it also tells the north exactly what kind of king has been crowned in the south. Godly and shrewd are not opposites; they are just harder to hold together than either alone.

Then the pool of Gibeon, and both armies are Israelite. Abner proposes a contest to keep a war small, and all twenty-four champions grab each other by the head and die in the same second, settling nothing — so the armies fight anyway. Asahel, who could run, chases the enemy commander in a straight line; Abner warns him twice, offers him an honourable way out, and finally jabs backwards with the blunt end of his spear to wind him. It goes straight through. Abner was still trying not to kill him at the moment he killed him.

And the best line of the day comes from the man most responsible for it: shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? Three hundred and eighty Israelites are dead at a water tank. Both armies then march all night in opposite directions, and nothing has been decided.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — David Inquired of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" The answer is yes; he asks a second question — to which shall I go up? — and is told Hebron (v. 1). He goes up with his two wives and every man and household, and the men of Judah anoint him king over the house of Judah (vv. 2-4). Told that it was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul, he sends them a blessing: may you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him... may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: He has the dead king's crown in his hands, an anointing from Samuel behind him, and a claim nobody could argue with — and he asks. Then, given a yes, he asks again rather than treat the first answer as covering the second. Set that beside 1 Sam. 27:1, where he said in his heart and moved six hundred families into enemy country for sixteen months.
verseByVerse.examples: And his first recorded act as king is a thank-you letter to the town that buried Saul. He uses the covenant word for what they did — the love that keeps going after the reason for it has gone — and asks God to show them the same. It is genuine, and it also tells every man in the north exactly what kind of king has just been crowned in the south.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron." So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David brought up his men who were with him, everyone with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron. And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul," David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him. Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing. Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron."'

Four words open the book's second chapter and they are the whole difference between this man and the last one: David inquired of the LORD.

Consider what he is holding while he asks.

He has the crown of the dead king, brought to him by the Amalekite. He has Samuel's anointing from a courtyard in Bethlehem years ago. Saul is dead, his heir is dead, and the northern army is destroyed. He has six hundred men, a reputation, and the tribe of Judah waiting. Nobody in the country could argue with the claim, and there is no living person he needs permission from.

He asks anyway.

And then he does something more instructive still. He gets a yes — go up — and he does not run with it. He asks a second question: to which shall I go up?

He will not treat the first answer as covering the second. Permission to move is not instruction about where, and he is not going to fill the gap himself and call the whole thing guidance.

Now set this against the last time we watched him make a large decision. Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines" (1 Sam. 27:1). No priest, no ephod, no prophet — and all three were in the camp. That sentence cost him sixteen months in enemy country and a page of his life he could not undo.

Same man. Opposite move. The difference is Ziklag: he asked for the ephod standing in the ashes of his own town (1 Sam. 30:7), and he has not stopped since.

Hebron is the right answer and he could not have known it. It is the oldest covenant ground in the country — Abraham bought the field and the cave there and buried Sarah in it, and Abraham and Isaac and Jacob are all in that ground (Gen. 23; 49:31). It is a Levitical city and a city of refuge, and it sits in the hill country at the centre of Judah's territory.

He is not told why. He is told where.

'So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David brought up his men who were with him, every man with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron.'

Six hundred households move at once, and the writer counts the wives.

Abigail is here, who came down a mountain track with two hundred loaves and talked him out of a massacre. Ahinoam is here. Michal, his first wife, is not: Saul gave her to another man while David was in the wilderness, and getting her back is going to be a condition in the next chapter.

'And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah.'

The third anointing, and each one has been from a different quarter.

Samuel poured the oil in his father's house in front of seven passed-over brothers, and nobody outside that room knew (1 Sam. 16:13). Now his own tribe does it publicly. And seven and a half years from now the elders of all Israel will come to Hebron and do it a third time (5:3).

God keeps confirming the same thing in front of larger and larger audiences, and each confirmation arrives only when the man has waited for it.

'When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul,"'

'David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him."'

His first recorded act as king is a thank-you letter to the men who buried his enemy.

Remember what they did. Jabesh-gilead is across the Jordan; Beth-shan, where Saul's body was nailed to the wall, is Philistine-held. Those men walked all night through occupied country, took four bodies down off a public wall, carried them home, burned them, buried the bones under a tamarisk and fasted for a week — for a king who had been failing them for years, with no possible reward, at real risk (1 Sam. 31:11-13).

And they did it because of one night forty years earlier, when Saul was a young man behind a plough and the Spirit of God rushed on him and he marched all night to save their town from an Ammonite who wanted every right eye in it (1 Sam. 11).

David sees exactly what that was and names it.

'"Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing."'

Steadfast love and faithfulness. The first word is hesed — the covenant word, love that keeps its promises when the reasons for keeping them have gone. It is what Jonathan asked David to show his descendants. It is what Abigail's whole speech turned on. It is what Jabesh-gilead did.

He asks God to do to them what they did to Saul.

'"Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."'

And then, at the end, the politics — and it would be dishonest to pretend it is not there.

He tells them Saul is dead and that Judah has crowned him, and he does not ask them for anything. That last sentence is information delivered to the most fiercely pro-Saul town in the country, by a man who has just praised them for their loyalty to Saul, and every word of it is calculated.

Both things are true at once, and the text is comfortable with that. The gratitude is real — he wrote a lament for Saul nobody made him write. And he is also a man who understands that the north is watching to see whether the new king in the south regards them as the enemy, and he has chosen the one gesture that answers the question before it is asked.

Godly and shrewd are not opposites. They are simply harder to hold together than either one on its own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Let the Young Men Compete Before Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abner takes Saul's surviving son Ish-bosheth across the Jordan to Mahanaim and makes him king over the north, while Judah follows David (vv. 8-10). Seven and a half years at Hebron (v. 11). The two forces meet at the pool of Gibeon and sit down on opposite sides of it (vv. 12-13). Abner proposes a contest: let the young men arise and compete before us (v. 14). Twelve against twelve step out — and each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together (vv. 15-16). The place is named the Field of Sword-Edges, and the battle was very fierce that day (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Both armies are Israelite. This is a civil war, and the men on either side of that pool were in the same muster a month ago. Ish-bosheth is a cipher — he makes one complaint in the whole book and is murdered in bed — and Abner is the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: The contest is a device for limiting a war, and twenty-four men kill each other simultaneously and settle nothing. That is what the place-name commemorates. Then the real fighting starts, and it runs for years.

verseByVerse.quote: But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim, and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months. Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool. And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise." Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David. And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon. And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim, and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel.'

Read the verbs. Abner took him, brought him over, and made him king.

Ish-bosheth does nothing in that sentence, and he does very little in the rest of the book. He speaks once, makes an accusation that destroys his own kingdom, and is murdered asleep in the afternoon. Abner is the reality; the son of Saul is the paperwork.

Note also where they go: Mahanaim, on the far side of the Jordan. The heartland is not safe enough to be crowned in.

'Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.'

Two years against seven and a half, and the arithmetic is doing something.

Ish-bosheth's reign is short and David's Hebron years are long, which means most of that period had no rival king in it at all. There is a gap the writer does not explain, and the effect is that David sat in Hebron for the better part of eight years as king of one tribe out of twelve, waiting. He had been waiting for about fifteen years already.

'Abner the son of Ner, servant of Ish-bosheth, and the servants of David went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool.'

Two armies sit down on opposite sides of a water tank and look at each other.

The pool at Gibeon has been dug out by archaeologists — a great shaft cut down through rock, with a spiral stair inside it, wide enough to be a landmark. It is a real place and this is a real afternoon, and the picture the sentence makes is of men waiting for somebody to decide something.

And they are all Israelites. That is the fact to keep hold of through this entire chapter and the next. Every man on both sides of that pool is a son of Jacob; some of them fought in the same line at Michmash. Joab is David's nephew and Abner is Saul's cousin, and the war they are about to start is a family quarrel with armies.

'And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise."'

The word is the ordinary one for a game.

What Abner proposes is a representative contest — a fixed number of champions from each side, the result standing for the whole. It was a recognised way of settling a matter without committing two armies, and everyone in the region understood it. Goliath had proposed exactly this in the Valley of Elah, and it had worked (1 Sam. 17:8-9).

So the intention is not bloodthirsty. Two generals who both know this war cannot really be won are looking for a way to keep the cost down.

Hold that, because of what happens next.

'Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.'

'And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon.'

All twenty-four die at once.

Read the sentence again, because it is one of the more terrible pieces of writing in the book and it is doing it entirely with choreography. Each man grabs his opposite number by the head and puts a sword in his side, and they go down in pairs. There is no winner. There is not even a fight worth describing. Twenty-four young men take hold of each other and die together in the same second.

Helkath-hazzurim means something like the Field of Sword-Edges, and Israel put that name on the ground and kept it.

Now think about what has just happened to Abner's plan. He proposed a contest to avoid a battle. The contest produced twenty-four dead and settled absolutely nothing, because there was nothing to settle — both teams lost.

'And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.'

So the armies go in anyway.

That is what came of the sensible plan for limiting the damage: the deaths of the twenty-four, and then the general engagement they were supposed to prevent, and then a war that runs for years.

There is a whole class of human decision in this. A measure adopted to contain a conflict becomes the thing that ignites it, because the men involved were never actually willing to accept a result they did not like. Abner would not have gone home if his twelve had lost. Neither would Joab. The tournament was a fiction they both agreed to while the swords were still sheathed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Turn Aside from Following Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asahel, Joab's brother, is as swift of foot as a wild gazelle, and he goes straight for Abner and will not turn to right or left (vv. 18-19). Abner tells him twice to break off — turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab? (vv. 21-22). He will not. So Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, and the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Abner is the most experienced soldier in Israel and he does not want this killing. He warns the boy twice, offers him an easier target, and names the exact reason: how could I lift up my face to your brother Joab? He can see the whole feud coming.
verseByVerse.examples: The blow is struck with the wrong end of the spear — a shove meant to wind a man and stop him, driven home by his own speed. It goes through him. That accident is the fuse for the murder at the gate in the next chapter, and for Joab's own execution forty years later (1 Kings 2:5-6).

verseByVerse.quote: And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle. And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner. Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I." Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him. And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?" But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle.'

The three brothers are named together, and they are David's nephews — Zeruiah is his sister. Between them they will run his army, win his wars, and cause him more trouble than any of his enemies.

Asahel is introduced by the one thing everybody knew about him. He could run.

'And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.'

He picks the commander-in-chief of the opposing army and goes after him in a straight line.

The phrase neither to the right hand nor to the left is normally a compliment in Scripture; it is what is said of a king who keeps the law. Here it describes a young man who has decided on a target and will not be talked out of it.

'Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I."'

Abner knows him by name. Of course he does — a month ago they were in the same country and possibly the same army, and everyone knew who the fast one was.

'Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.'

The first warning, and note the shape of it: not go home but take somebody else. He is offering the boy an honourable way out with plunder in his hands, so that nothing has to be explained afterwards.

'And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?"'

The second warning, and the reason given is the whole future of the book.

How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?

Abner is the most experienced soldier alive in Israel and he can see exactly what is coming. Not the tactical situation — he could kill this boy in a second and both of them know it — but what follows. Blood between families does not stay where it falls. If he kills Asahel, Joab will come for him, and it will not matter what the circumstances were.

He is not begging for his life. He is warning a young man that his death will start something neither of them can stop.

And Asahel keeps running.

'So Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, and the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was.'

With the butt of his spear.

That detail is the whole of Abner's intention and it is easy to read past. He does not turn and put the point through him. He jabs backwards with the blunt end — the counterweight at the base of the shaft — which is what you do to wind a man, knock the breath out of him, and stop him without killing him.

And it goes straight through, because Asahel was running flat out and ran onto it. The spear comes out at his back.

Abner was still trying not to kill him at the moment he killed him.

'And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.'

The pursuit stops. Men come round the shoulder of the hill, see who is lying there, and cannot go on.

That single line does more than a paragraph of description. Everyone who arrives knows the face, knows whose brother he is, and understands in the same instant what has just been set in motion.

Because this is the fuse. Everything that happens to Abner in the next chapter happens because of this afternoon: Joab will call him aside at the gate of Hebron as though to speak with him privately, and put a blade in his stomach — the same wound, in the same place, returned.

And that murder is not the end of it either. Forty years later, dying, David will still be talking about it, and will tell Solomon what to do about Joab: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war (1 Kings 2:5-6). Joab dies holding the horns of the altar.

All of it comes out of a boy who could run fast and would not turn aside.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–32 — Shall the Sword Devour Forever?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab and Abishai pursue until sundown, and Abner's men rally on a hilltop (vv. 24-25). Then Abner calls down: shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? How long will you refrain from telling your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers? (v. 26). Joab answers that if he had not spoken, the pursuit would have gone on till morning — blows the trumpet, and stops (vv. 27-28). Abner marches all night back across the Jordan (v. 29). The count: nineteen of David's men and Asahel; three hundred and sixty of Abner's (vv. 30-31). They bury Asahel at Bethlehem and march all night to Hebron (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The pursuit of their brothers. Abner names what this is, and he is the man who started it that morning with a proposal for a tournament. The best sentence in the chapter comes from the person most responsible for the day.
verseByVerse.examples: Both sides then march all night in opposite directions, one to a burial at Bethlehem and one across the Jordan. Nothing has been decided and three hundred and eighty-one Israelites are dead.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill. Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?" And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning." So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore. And Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim. Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel. But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men. And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.'

The dead brother's two brothers keep going, and the chase runs all afternoon.

'And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill.'

Abner's men rally, and the pursuit has now caught up with a formed body on high ground, which means the next thing will be expensive for everybody.

'Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? How long will you refrain from telling your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?"'

That is the best thing anybody says in this chapter, and it comes out of the mouth of the man who caused the day.

Take it in three parts.

Shall the sword devour forever? The picture is of a weapon that eats — a thing with an appetite of its own that does not stop when the reason for drawing it has been met. Anybody who has watched a quarrel outlive its cause knows the image is exact.

Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? He is not appealing to mercy. He is telling a professional soldier something a professional soldier already knows: this ends badly for your side too, and the taste of it lasts.

The pursuit of their brothers.

There is the word, and it is the true description of the whole day. Not enemies. Brothers. The men on that hill and the men at the bottom of it are the same nation, and everybody has been pretending otherwise since breakfast.

Now the honesty the passage requires. Abner started this. He proposed the contest at the pool that morning; twenty-four young men are dead because of a suggestion he made; and he has spent the afternoon losing a battle he chose to fight. He is also, at this precise moment, calling for peace from a hilltop because he is about to be overrun.

All of that is true, and the sentence is still true. Right words are not always spoken by disinterested people, and self-interest does not automatically make a thing false. Abner is manoeuvring, and he is also correct, and Joab knows it.

'And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning."'

Joab's answer is colder than it looks, and it repays a second reading.

He does not disagree. He picks up Abner's own phrase — the pursuit of their brothers — and says that if Abner had not spoken, it would have gone on all night.

Which is either a complaint or a confession, and probably both. He is saying: I would not have stopped. You stopped me. And there is not a word in it about Asahel, from a man who has just spent the afternoon chasing the person who killed his brother, and who will settle that account in the next chapter with a knife.

'So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore.'

He stops it, and he stops it immediately. Whatever else is true of Joab — and a great deal is — he is not a man who loses control of himself or his troops.

'And Abner and his men went all night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim.'

'Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel. But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men.'

The count is given, and the writer counts both sides.

Nineteen and Asahel. Three hundred and sixty. Three hundred and eighty Israelites dead in one afternoon at a water tank, and one name among them — because that is the one that will cost more than all the rest put together.

Note that David's side won convincingly, nearly nineteen to one. It changed nothing. There will be another five or six years of this.

'And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.'

The chapter ends with two night marches going in opposite directions.

Abner is crossing the Jordan in the dark to get home to Mahanaim. Joab is carrying his brother's body to Bethlehem, burying him in their father's tomb, and then walking through the night to Hebron, and the sun comes up on him as he arrives.

Both armies spend the same night walking away from a battle that decided nothing. It is a bleak, exact ending, and the writer offers no comment on any of it.

The kingdom is coming to David. This is what it costs while it comes, and most of the cost is being paid by people who never chose either side.

2.theology:
He asks, and then he asks again (v. 1). The claim was unarguable and the moment was obvious, and he still put it to God — and having been told go up, he would not treat that as an answer to where. Permission to move is not instruction about direction, and he refuses to fill the gap himself and call the result guidance. The contrast is exact and the writer means it: 1 Sam. 27:1, David said in his heart, with a priest, an ephod and a prophet all sitting in his own camp. What changed was Ziklag, where he called for the ephod standing in the ashes.

Hebron, and being told where but not why (v. 1). It is the oldest covenant ground in the country — Abraham's purchased field, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob all buried in it (Gen. 23; 49:31) — a Levitical city and a city of refuge at the centre of Judah. He could not have reasoned his way to it, and he is given the destination without the argument for it.

Three anointings, each to a wider audience (v. 4). Samuel's oil in a private house that nobody outside the room knew about (1 Sam. 16:13); now his own tribe, publicly; and in seven and a half years the elders of all Israel at this same Hebron (5:3). God keeps confirming the same word in front of larger audiences, and each confirmation arrives only after the waiting.

The thank-you to Jabesh-gilead (vv. 5-7). He uses hesed of what they did and asks God to show them the same — and then, at the end, tells them Saul is dead and Judah has crowned him, which is a political sentence delivered to the most pro-Saul town in Israel. Both are true at once and the text is comfortable with it. The gratitude is real; he wrote a lament nobody made him write. He is also a man who knows the north is watching, and who picks the one gesture that answers the question before it is asked.

Abner is the kingdom (vv. 8-10). Read the verbs: Abner took Ish-bosheth, brought him over, made him king. The son of Saul speaks once in the whole book, destroys his own throne with the sentence, and is murdered asleep in the afternoon. And they are crowned at Mahanaim, across the Jordan, because the heartland is not safe.

A measure to contain a war becomes the thing that starts it (vv. 14-17). Representative combat was a recognised way of settling a matter without two armies — Goliath had proposed it in the Valley of Elah. Here twenty-four men catch each other by the head and go down in pairs in the same second, and there is no winner and nothing settled, so the armies engage anyway. The tournament was a fiction both generals agreed to while the swords were sheathed; neither would have gone home on a losing result.

Abner did not want to kill him (vv. 21-23). Two warnings, an honourable alternative with plunder attached, and a reason stated out loud — how then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab? He can see the feud from where he is standing. And the blow is struck with the butt of the spear, the blunt counterweight, which is what you use to wind a man and stop him. Asahel's own speed drives it through. Then the whole pursuit halts: men come round the hill, see the face, and cannot go on. That afternoon runs forward to a knife at the gate of Hebron in the next chapter and to Joab dying at the altar forty years later (1 Kings 2:5-6).

The right words from an interested party (v. 26). Abner proposed the contest, twenty-four men are dead because of it, and he is calling for peace from a hilltop because he is about to be overrun. All of that is true and the sentence is still true: the sword does devour, it is bitter in the end, and they are brothers. Self-interest does not automatically make a thing false, and Joab — who answers by admitting he would not have stopped — knows it.
2.examples:
Then: Two Israelite armies sat down on opposite sides of a rock-cut water tank and agreed to settle the matter with twelve men a side — and every one of the twenty-four caught his opposite number by the head and put a sword in his ribs at the same instant, so that they fell in pairs and nothing at all was decided. They named the ground the Field of Sword-Edges and then fought the battle anyway.

Now: Two things. Verse 1 is the practical one: David got a clear yes and still would not assume it answered the next question. Most bad decisions made by people who genuinely want to obey are made in exactly that gap — a real leading about whether, quietly extended to cover where, when and how, until a great deal is being done on an authority that was never given. And Abner's line is the other: a quarrel does not stop when its cause is met, because the sword has an appetite of its own. Somebody usually has to call across the valley and say so, and it is very often the person least entitled to.

3.title: Abner's Defection and Joab's Revenge
3.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker.<sup>2</sup>And sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam of Jezreel;<sup>3</sup>and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;<sup>4</sup>and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital;<sup>5</sup>and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.<sup>6</sup>While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul.<sup>7</sup>Now Saul had a concubine whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?"<sup>8</sup>Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, "Am I a dog's head of Judah? To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not given you into the hand of David. And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman.<sup>9</sup>God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him,<sup>10</sup>to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."<sup>11</sup>And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.<sup>12</sup>And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and behold, my hand shall be with you to bring over all Israel to you."<sup>13</sup>And he said, "Good; I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you; that is, you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see my face."<sup>14</sup>Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, for whom I paid the bridal price of a hundred foreskins of the Philistines."<sup>15</sup>And Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel the son of Laish.<sup>16</sup>But her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned.<sup>17</sup>And Abner conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you.<sup>18</sup>Now then bring it about, for the LORD has promised David, saying, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from the hand of all their enemies.'"<sup>19</sup>Abner also spoke to Benjamin. And then Abner went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin thought good to do.<sup>20</sup>When Abner came with twenty men to David at Hebron, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him.<sup>21</sup>And Abner said to David, "I will arise and go and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.<sup>22</sup>Just then the servants of David arrived with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.<sup>23</sup>When Joab and all the army that was with him came, it was told Joab, "Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has let him go, and he has gone in peace."<sup>24</sup>Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, so that he is gone?<sup>25</sup>You know that Abner the son of Ner came to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing."<sup>26</sup>When Joab came out from David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. But David did not know about it.<sup>27</sup>And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.<sup>28</sup>Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner the son of Ner.<sup>29</sup>May it fall upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house, and may the house of Joab never be without one who has a discharge or who is leprous or who holds a spindle or who falls by the sword or who lacks bread!"<sup>30</sup>So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.<sup>31</sup>Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David followed the bier.<sup>32</sup>They buried Abner at Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept.<sup>33</sup>And the king lamented for Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies?<sup>34</sup>Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen." And all the people wept again over him.<sup>35</sup>Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David swore, saying, "God do so to me and more also, if I taste bread or anything else till the sun goes down!"<sup>36</sup>And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people.<sup>37</sup>So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner the son of Ner.<sup>38</sup>And the king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?<sup>39</sup>And I was gentle today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"
3.overview:
One flat verse covers years of civil war and gives away the ending: stronger and stronger, weaker and weaker. Then a list of six sons by six mothers, dropped in like an administrative note — and three of those names are the rest of the book. Amnon will rape his half-sister; Absalom will murder Amnon and drive his father out of Jerusalem; Adonijah will grab at the throne while David lies dying. The law had said it in one sentence: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. And Absalom's mother is a foreign princess from Geshur — which is exactly where Absalom will run after the murder.

Ish-bosheth accuses Abner over Saul's concubine, which sounds domestic and is constitutional: taking a dead king's women was the recognised claim on his throne. Abner does not deny it. What he does is quote God — what the LORD has sworn to him — and the sentence should stop the reader, because it means he knew. He fought at Gilboa, crowned a rival, and ran a seven-year war knowing. What moves him at last is not conviction but being spoken to disrespectfully about a woman.

David's one condition is Michal, and both his motives are real and the text will not sort them out. Nobody asks her anything. Her husband Paltiel walks behind the party weeping as far as Bahurim, is told two words by a general, and turns round and goes home. That verse is the hardest thing in the chapter and Scripture does not excuse it.

Then Joab. He accuses Abner of spying with no evidence at all, sends messengers in the king's name without the king's knowledge, and murders him in the gate at Hebron — which is a city of refuge, the one place in Israel where a man who killed without intent was legally safe, and Abner's killing of Asahel is the textbook case those cities existed for. He does it by the offer of a private word, with the same wound in the same place. David curses him, walks behind the coffin, weeps at the grave, sings a lament, refuses food — and does nothing else. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — What the LORD Has Sworn to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker (v. 1). Six sons are born to him at Hebron, by six different women — Amnon, Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, Ithream (vv. 2-5). Then Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of going in to Rizpah, Saul's concubine, and Abner's fury breaks the northern kingdom in half: God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba (vv. 7-10). And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: That list of sons is a bomb with a long fuse. Amnon will rape his half-sister; Absalom will murder Amnon and then take the kingdom by force; Adonijah will try to take it again as David lies dying. Every one of them has a different mother, and the law had told Israel's king plainly not to multiply wives (Deut. 17:17).
verseByVerse.examples: And Abner says the quiet part out loud. He has known what God swore, all along, through every year of the war he has been running. He is not converted in verse 9; he is insulted, and he moves to the side he always knew would win.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker. And sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam of Jezreel; and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital; and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron. While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul. Now Saul had a concubine whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?" To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not given you into the hand of David. And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman. God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba." And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker.'

One verse covers years, and it does two things at once.

It tells us this went on a long time. Not a season of skirmishing — a war, between two halves of the same nation, with the pool of Gibeon somewhere near the beginning of it.

And it tells us the outcome before it happens, in the flattest possible way. Stronger and stronger; weaker and weaker. There is no drama in the sentence at all, and that is the point. What God said would happen is happening, at the pace of ordinary events, while people fight about it.

'And sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam of Jezreel; and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;'

'and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital; and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.'

Six sons. Six mothers. And the writer drops the list into the middle of a war report as though it were an administrative note.

Read the names again slowly, because three of them are the rest of this book.

Amnon will rape his half-sister Tamar and be murdered at a sheep-shearing feast two years later (ch. 13). Absalom will do the murdering, flee to his grandfather in Geshur, come back, steal the hearts of Israel at the city gate, drive his father out of Jerusalem barefoot, sleep with his father's concubines on the palace roof in daylight, and die hanging in an oak with three javelins in his chest (chs. 13-18). Adonijah will try to take the throne while David lies dying, and be executed by Solomon (1 Kings 1-2).

Every one of them by a different woman.

The law had said this to Israel's king, in advance, in one sentence: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). It is not a rule about appetite. A household of rival women and rival sons is a household of factions, and a royal household of factions is a civil war with a nursery.

Note also who Absalom's mother is: Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. A foreign princess, which means the marriage was a treaty. And when Absalom kills his brother and runs, he runs to Geshur, to his grandfather, and stays three years (13:37-38). The alliance David made to secure a border produced the son who nearly took his throne, and the bolt-hole the son escaped to.

The narrator says none of this. He gives a list of names between a war summary and a palace quarrel, and lets it sit.

'While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul.'

'Now Saul had a concubine whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?"'

The accusation looks domestic and it is constitutional.

In that world, taking a dead king's women was a claim on his throne, and everybody understood it. It is not a private matter that happens to be embarrassing; it is the recognised public gesture for saying the succession is mine. Absalom will do it deliberately, on a roof, in front of the whole city, on Ahithophel's advice, precisely because it is unmistakable (16:21-22).

So Ish-bosheth is accusing his general of moving on the crown, and he may well be right.

He is also finished the moment he says it. Abner is the army, the administration and the reason Ish-bosheth is king at all. Insulting him is the only decision this man makes in the entire book, and it destroys him.

'Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, "Am I a dog's head of Judah? To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not given you into the hand of David. And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman."'

He does not deny it.

Read the answer again. It is a list of services rendered and a complaint about ingratitude, and nowhere in it does he say the thing did not happen. What he says is: after everything I have done for your father's house, you are going to raise this?

A dog's head is about as low as the insults of that culture went, and the sneer at Judah is deliberate.

'"God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."'

There is the sentence that should stop anybody reading this chapter.

What the LORD has sworn to him.

Abner has known. Not suspected — known, and known that God swore it. He can quote it, including the geography, from Dan to Beersheba, which is the whole country from top to bottom.

Now count what he has done with that knowledge. He fought at Gilboa for a king God had rejected. He took Saul's surviving son across the Jordan and crowned him. He ran a civil war for years against the man God had sworn to enthrone. Three hundred and eighty Israelites died at the pool of Gibeon because of a proposal he made, and Asahel died on the end of his spear.

All of it knowing.

And what changes his mind is not conviction, not repentance, not the word of God he has just quoted. It is being spoken to disrespectfully about a woman.

Sit with that, because it is more common than the dramatic version. Very few people who resist what they know to be right are converted by an argument. They are moved when the arrangement they were defending finally insults them, and then they discover that they had known all along, and they say so, loudly, as though the knowledge were new.

God's purpose goes forward through it. He is using a furious general with wounded pride and no change of heart whatever, and the kingdom moves a step closer to the man he has been trying to kill for seven years.

'And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.'

The last thing recorded about this king is that he could not think of anything to say.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abner opens negotiations, and David's answer has one condition: you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter (vv. 12-13). He sends the same demand to Ish-bosheth, naming the bride-price he paid (v. 14). She is taken from her husband — but her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned (vv. 15-16). Abner then works the elders of Israel and of Benjamin, reminding them they had wanted David for years (vv. 17-19), comes to Hebron with twenty men, is given a feast, and leaves in peace (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Michal is Saul's daughter, so the marriage attaches David's claim to the old dynasty; she is also his first wife, taken from him by force while he was in the wilderness. Both motives are real, and the text does not sort them out.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody asks Michal anything. And the one line given to Paltiel — walking behind her as far as Bahurim, weeping, and then told to go home, and going — is the whole cost of the transaction, recorded and left standing without a word of justification.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and behold, my hand shall be with you to bring over all Israel to you." And he said, "Good; I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you; that is, you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see my face." Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, for whom I paid the bridal price of a hundred foreskins of the Philistines." And Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel the son of Laish. But her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned. And Abner conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you. Now then bring it about, for the LORD has promised David, saying, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from the hand of all their enemies.'" Abner also spoke to Benjamin. And then Abner went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin thought good to do. When Abner came with twenty men to David at Hebron, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him. And Abner said to David, "I will arise and go and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and behold, my hand shall be with you to bring over all Israel to you."'

He opens with a rhetorical question and follows it with an offer, and both are the work of a man who knows his own value.

To whom does the land belong? He means: we both know the answer, and we both know I am the only person who can deliver it.

'And he said, "Good; I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you; that is, you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see my face."'

One condition, and it is a woman.

Michal. Saul's younger daughter, who loved David — the narrator said so outright, and it is the only place in the Old Testament where a woman is said to love a man. She warned him the night the assassins came, let him down through a window on a rope, put an idol in his bed with goats' hair at its head to buy him time, and lied to her father's face about it (1 Sam. 18:20; 19:11-17).

Then Saul gave her to another man while David was in the wilderness, as though the marriage had never happened (1 Sam. 25:44).

Why does David want her back? Both reasons are real and the text will not sort them out.

She is Saul's daughter, and a king of Judah married to Saul's daughter is a king with a claim in the north that the northern tribes can recognise. That is politics, and it is the reason he raises it in a negotiation about the kingdom rather than at any point in the previous seven years.

And she was his wife, taken from him by force by a man who was trying to kill him, and he has never accepted it. That is not nothing.

'Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, whom I betrothed at the price of a hundred foreskins of the Philistines."'

He goes over Abner's head to the king as well, so the transfer is legally clean, and he cites the bride-price.

That price was Saul's idea, and its purpose was to get David killed — a hundred Philistines was expected to be the end of him (1 Sam. 18:25). He brought two hundred. David is reminding the house of Saul that he paid what Saul asked, twice over, and that the marriage was lawful.

'And Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel the son of Laish.'

'But her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned.'

One verse, and it is the hardest thing in the chapter.

Paltiel gets no dialogue, no protest, no argument. He walks behind the party, crying, for what is perhaps a dozen miles, until a general who has killed men with a spear tells him two words. And he turns round and goes home.

He had been married to her for years. Nobody consulted him and nobody compensated him. There is no suggestion he did anything wrong; he was given a wife by his king and he loved her, and now two governments have agreed on something and he is walking back to Gallim on his own.

Nobody asks Michal.

She is not addressed by anyone at any point. She is taken from her husband by Ish-bosheth, delivered by Abner, and handed to David, and she does not speak in this chapter or the next. The last time she spoke she was lying to her father to save David's life. The next time she speaks, three chapters from now, it will be to despise him from a window, and the writer will tell us she had no children to the day of her death (6:16-23).

Something happened to that woman between the window with the rope and the window in Jerusalem, and this chapter is a large part of it.

It would be easy, and wrong, to hurry past this. Scripture does not excuse it, and neither should a reader. David is not accused here by the narrator — but the narrator does not usually accuse anybody, and he has just made sure we watch a man weep for twelve miles.

'And Abner conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you. Now then bring it about, for the LORD has promised David, saying, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from the hand of all their enemies.'"'

He works the elders, and he does it by telling them what they already wanted.

For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you. So the northern enthusiasm for David was there all along, and Abner was the man holding it back. He now presents himself as the one making it possible.

And again he quotes God. A second oracle, this time about salvation from the Philistines. He has the theology at his fingertips and always did.

'Abner also spoke to Benjamin. And then Abner went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin thought good to do.'

Benjamin gets a separate conversation, because Benjamin is Saul's own tribe and has the most to lose.

'When Abner came with twenty men to David at Hebron, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him. And Abner said to David, "I will arise and go and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.'

And he went in peace.

The phrase is repeated three times in the next six verses, which is the writer leaning on something. Abner came under safe conduct, ate at the king's table, and left with the king's word on him.

Everything that is about to happen is a violation of that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — In the Midst of the Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab comes back from a raid, learns Abner has been received and sent away in peace, and confronts the king: you know that Abner the son of Ner came to deceive you (vv. 22-25). Then he sends messengers after Abner — but David did not know about it (v. 26). And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother (v. 27). David hears, declares himself and his kingdom forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner, and curses Joab's house (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Hebron is a city of refuge (Josh. 20:7) — the one place in Israel where a man who killed without intent was legally protected from the avenger of blood. And Abner's killing of Asahel, with two warnings and the blunt end of a spear, is precisely the case those cities existed for. Joab commits the murder inside the sanctuary, in the gate, which is where justice was done.
verseByVerse.examples: And he does it by the pretence of a private word, with a wound to the stomach — the same wound, in the same place, that killed Asahel at Gibeon.

verseByVerse.quote: Just then the servants of David arrived with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace. When Joab and all the army that was with him came, it was told Joab, "Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has let him go, and he has gone in peace." Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, so that he is gone? You know that Abner the son of Ner came to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing." When Joab came out from David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. But David did not know about it. And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother. Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner the son of Ner. May it fall upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house, and may the house of Joab never be without one who has a discharge or who is leprous or who holds a spindle or who falls by the sword or who lacks bread!" So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Just then the servants of David arrived with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.'

Joab has been out of town. The timing is not an accident of the story; it is the reason there was a deal at all.

'When Joab and all the army that was with him came, it was told Joab, "Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has let him go, and he has gone in peace."'

'Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, so that he is gone? You know that Abner the son of Ner came to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing."'

He speaks to the king of Judah like that, in his own house, and nothing happens to him.

The charge is that Abner was a spy. There is not a word anywhere in the chapter to support it, and Joab does not offer any evidence. It is the argument available, not the reason.

The reason is a body in a tomb at Bethlehem. Abner killed Asahel at Gibeon, and Joab buried his brother and walked all night to Hebron and has been waiting ever since.

There is also a second motive, and it would be naive to leave it out. If Abner delivers the northern tribes, Abner becomes the most important man in the kingdom after the king, and Joab is currently the most important man in the kingdom after the king. The spy story is a pretext for a blood feud, and the blood feud is running alongside a promotion he does not intend to lose.

'When Joab came out from David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. But David did not know about it.'

But David did not know about it.

The writer puts that in deliberately, and it is the hinge of the whole affair. Everything that follows is done in the king's name, with the king's messengers, from the king's town, without the king's knowledge.

Abner turns round and comes back because he has no reason not to. He has eaten at David's table and been sent away in peace. A summons from Hebron means the king wants another word.

'And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.'

Now take that verse apart, because there are four separate outrages inside it and the narrator states all four without raising his voice.

The first is the place. Hebron. Turn to Joshua 20 and there is a list of six cities set aside by God's own command as cities of refuge, and Hebron is the first one named in the south (Josh. 20:7). Their purpose was exact: a man who killed somebody without intent could run to one of them and be safe from the avenger of blood until there had been a proper hearing.

And Abner's killing of Asahel is the textbook case. He warned the boy twice, offered him another target, said out loud that he did not want to face Joab afterwards, and struck backwards with the blunt end of a spear to wind him. Asahel's own speed drove it through. If any death in Scripture was manslaughter rather than murder, it is that one.

The city that existed to protect exactly this man is where he is killed for exactly this death.

The second is the spot. Into the midst of the gate. The gate was the courthouse. It is where the elders sat, where property changed hands, where a case was heard and witnesses stood — Boaz settled the redemption of Ruth in a gate with ten elders watching. It is the most public and most legally protected ground in the town.

The third is the method. To speak with him privately. He is murdered by the offer of a confidential word — the exact gesture of trust, used as the weapon. Abner has to lean in for it to work.

The fourth is the wound. He struck him in the stomach. That is where Abner's spear went into Asahel, and everybody involved would have known it. It is not a killing; it is a transaction.

Joab is not a hot-tempered man. He waited, he chose the ground, and he made every part of it a mirror.

'Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner the son of Ner."'

His first concern is guilt, and specifically corporate guilt.

This is not a press statement, though it functions as one. In Israel, shed blood defiled the land and lay on the community until it was answered, and a killing done by the king's commander in the king's city with the king's messengers would ordinarily lie on the king. David is declaring before God that it does not.

'"May it fall upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house, and may the house of Joab never be without one who has a discharge or who is leprous or who holds a spindle or who falls by the sword or who lacks bread!"'

Then he curses him, comprehensively and permanently, and does absolutely nothing else.

That gap is the point of the chapter's last verse, and we will come to it.

'So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.'

The narrator gives the plain verdict, names both brothers, and states the motive without any of Joab's varnish.

Not espionage. Not the security of the kingdom. Because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.

And note the last three words. In the battle. The writer says it himself: this was a death in war, and Joab has answered it in peacetime, which is the precise thing David will still be naming on his deathbed forty years later (1 Kings 2:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–39 — The Sons of Zeruiah Are More Severe Than I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David orders Joab himself to tear his clothes and walk in the procession, and King David followed the bier (v. 31). At the grave he weeps aloud and sings: should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen (vv. 32-34). He refuses food until sundown, and all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them (vv. 35-36). So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner (v. 37). Then to his servants: do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel? — and I was gentle today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I (vv. 38-39).
verseByVerse.theology: Should Abner die as a fool dies? The protest is about the manner of it. He was not taken in battle and he was not a prisoner — his hands were free and his feet were free, and he walked into a gate expecting a conversation.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 39 is David naming his own weakness in public, and it is the truest thing he says all chapter. He cannot control Joab. He will not be able to control him when Joab kills Absalom against a direct order (18:14) or murders Amasa the same way (20:10), and in the end he can only hand the problem to Solomon from his deathbed (1 Kings 2:5-6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David followed the bier. They buried Abner at Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept. And the king lamented for Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen." And all the people wept again over him. Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David swore, saying, "God do so to me and more also, if I taste bread or anything else till the sun goes down!" And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people. So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner the son of Ner. And the king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel? And I was gentle today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David followed the bier.'

He makes the murderer walk in the funeral.

Joab is ordered to tear his clothes, put on sackcloth and mourn in public for the man he killed the day before, in front of the whole town. It is not justice and David knows it is not justice. It is the only thing he can make him do.

Then the king walks behind the coffin.

Think about who is in that procession. David is following the bier of the general who fought against him for seven years, crowned a rival, ran the war, and killed his own nephew. He is grieving for the commander of the opposing army, publicly, at the head of his people.

'They buried Abner at Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept.'

'And the king lamented for Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen."'

A second lament, and this is the second poem in three chapters David has composed for a man on the other side.

Should Abner die as a fool dies?

The protest is not that he died. It is how. A soldier of that rank should fall in the line with a weapon in his hand, and there is an honour in that which his whole world recognised.

Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered. He was not a prisoner. He had not been taken, tried, condemned, or led out. He was a free man walking into a gate under safe conduct to hear what the king wanted.

As one falls before the wicked you have fallen. That is the verdict, and the word is aimed at somebody standing in the crowd in sackcloth.

'And all the people wept again over him. Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David swore, saying, "God do so to me and more also, if I taste bread or anything else till the sun goes down!"'

He fasts, and he swears an oath about it in front of everybody.

'And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people.'

'So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner the son of Ner.'

There is what the whole day was for.

It has to be said plainly that this is politics as well as grief, because the text says so. The narrator tells us what the people concluded, and that is the outcome the day was designed to produce.

Think about the position David is in. Abner has just persuaded the northern tribes to come over, and forty-eight hours later Abner is dead in David's own city, killed by David's own commander, brought back by messengers who came from David's house. Every man in the north is asking one question, and if the answer they settle on is the king had him killed, the union is finished before it starts and the war goes on for another decade.

So David makes it impossible to believe. He curses Joab publicly, walks behind the coffin himself, weeps at the graveside in front of witnesses, composes a lament, and swears an oath not to eat.

And here is the thing that has to be held alongside it: none of that means the grief is false. The man wrote a lament for Saul with nothing in it for himself, and he wrote this one too. He is capable of meaning every word and of knowing exactly what it will accomplish, at the same time, which is what it is to be a public man with a real heart.

The alternative was available and it was easy. He could have said nothing, accepted the convenient death of the one man who might have rivalled Joab, and let people think what they liked. Plenty of kings would have. It would have cost him the north.

'And the king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?"'

A prince and a great man. Said of an enemy general, to his own staff, on the record.

David has a habit by now, and it should be named: he is very good at saying the true good thing about people who have cost him a great deal. Saul got scarlet and gold and eagles. Abner gets a prince and a great man. Neither of them had earned it from him personally.

'"And I was gentle today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"'

The last verse of the chapter is David admitting he cannot control his own army, and it is the most honest sentence he speaks all day.

I was gentle today, though anointed king. The word can also mean weak, and he is not paying himself a compliment. He is saying: I am the anointed king of Judah and a murder was committed under my nose by my own commander and I have done nothing about it except make him wear sackcloth.

These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. His own nephews. Joab and Abishai are harder men than he is, they command the loyalty of the army, and he needs them.

The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness. Which is the same move he made in the cave at Engedi — may the LORD judge between me and you — and it is not the same situation at all. There he was a fugitive with no power and handing the case to God was faith. Here he is the king, the law is his to administer, and handing the case to God is a way of not doing his job.

Scripture lets that stand without comment, and the rest of the book is the bill.

Joab, unpunished, will run David's army for forty more years. He will murder Amasa in exactly the same way — a friendly greeting, a hand on the beard, a blade in the stomach (20:9-10). He will kill Absalom with three javelins while the boy hangs helpless in a tree, in direct defiance of an order the whole army heard (18:5, 14). He will speak to David as no subject should speak to a king, and get away with it, because he knows too much and holds too much.

And at the end, on his deathbed, David will hand the whole unfinished business to a young man who has the strength to do what he never did: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me... Act therefore according to your wisdom, and do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace (1 Kings 2:5-6).

Forty years is a long time to carry a thing you should have dealt with on the day. David named his own weakness accurately in verse 39, in public, and then lived inside it for the rest of his reign.

3.theology:
The bomb with a long fuse (vv. 2-5). Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah are all in this list and all three tear the house apart. Deuteronomy 17:17 is not a rule about appetite: a household of rival women and rival sons is a household of factions, and a royal household of factions is a civil war with a nursery. And the treaty marriage that secured a border produced both the son who nearly took the throne and the bolt-hole he escaped to (13:37-38). The narrator states none of it — he puts a list of names between a war summary and a palace quarrel and lets it sit.

Abner knew all along (v. 9). He can quote what God swore, including the geography. He fought at Gilboa for a rejected king, crowned Saul's son across the Jordan, and ran a war for years against the man God had sworn to enthrone — and three hundred and eighty Israelites died at Gibeon over a proposal he made.
